character_and_relationship_context: Aminata Diallo is a young woman living in the city, where she rents a cramped room with two other apprentices, Serge, who is learning plumbing, and Mariam, who is learning tiling. She wakes at 4:30 each morning, boils millet porridge over a kerosene stove, and sells it at a nearby construction site, carrying the pot on her head and serving precisely measured amounts. She counts her coins carefully and keeps them in a cloth pouch tied to her waist. She never gives credit, even to foremen, and smiles politely while refusing. She attends a government-run trade school in the afternoons, where she is learning plastering. In the plastering workshop, she practices spreading plaster onto half-finished walls, tests consistency with her finger, and photographs her finished walls with a secondhand cellphone, keeping the photos in a folder labeled 'walls.' In the evenings, she reviews these photos, comparing trowel marks, noting flaws, and sketching corrections in a small notebook. She is cautious with her words, speaks in short, measured sentences, and watches others closely to learn from their techniques. She keeps her savings in a tin box hidden under her mattress, counts them each Sunday, and then burns the written total. She does not trust banks, having witnessed a bank collapse in her hometown when she was twelve, which led to a neighbor losing her funeral savings. She is cautious about people but not unkind: she occasionally shares porridge with a stray dog and helps Mariam carry heavy bags of tile, yet she never reveals the exact amount she saves or discusses her family. She left her village two years ago after a failed harvest, with her eldest uncle suggesting marriage, but she convinced her mother to allow her to learn a trade, inspired by a woman smoothing cement walls. Her roommates are her only close peers in the city; they share rent and chores, but neither knows about her savings or family background. Serge teases her about her photo folder but lends her his trowel when hers dulls. Mariam encourages her to rest and helped her carry tile after a backache last month.
objective_situation: It is evening in the cramped room Aminata shares with Serge and Mariam. Dinner is finished. Serge has pulled out a worn deck of cards, and Mariam is spreading a cloth on the floor. They both turn to Aminata, who is already sitting on her mattress with her cellphone in hand, the photo folder open. Mariam says, 'Come play a few rounds, you're always working.' Aminata looks at the screen showing her last plastered wall, then at the inviting circle on the floor. She can either join them for the evening or continue her usual review of wall photos and notes before bed.
state_and_available_memories: Aminata's right shoulder aches from plastering practice, and she is fuller than usual from dinner. The photo screen shows a wall she is proud of but knows has a flaw near the window. She has not yet looked at tomorrow's assignment list. On weekday evenings, she usually reviews wall photos and sketches corrections for at least an hour before bed, even when invited to card games. She has declined the past three card-game invitations to finish her notes. When she does join, she plays one round and returns to her mattress and phone. The worn card deck brings back the deck her uncle used for betting at village harvests, a game she refused to learn. Mariam's sing-song call echoes how her mother called her brothers in from fieldwork, pulling her attention. Her own photo of the wall reminds her of the instructor pointing out a dip while praising her corners. She remembers her mother's story of a neighbor who lost her market stall money because she spent evenings playing cards instead of sewing. She recalls one evening two weeks ago when she joined the game and the next day made a ceiling-corner mistake, setting her back. But she also remembers that after a rare full evening of cards last month, she woke with clear focus and her porridge sales went well.
name: Aminata Diallo
